extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic, philosophy, and inductive reasoning; scholars learning to detect and avoid fallacies of generalization
extracted.subtask_description: Enumerating and explaining the principal fallacies that corrupt inductive reasoning and generalization, with examples and guidance on avoiding them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish perceptions from inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: The frequent confusion between what is directly perceived and the inferences drawn from those perceptions; witnesses and untrained observers tend to mix hypothesis with narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious to separate the bare sensory report from any explanatory hypothesis. Train analytic habits of distinguishing sensation from inference (painters and psychologists practice this). Examples and warning: cross-examiners find witnesses intermix inferences; ignorant observers’ descriptions often contain theoretical phraseology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not generalize from local order to the distant universe
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations from the order of nature on Earth or within the solar system to remote parts of the universe are groundless unless warranted, because phenomena elsewhere may obey different laws or none at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extrapolating earthly regularities to unknown regions without special evidence; empirical observation confined to a limited domain does not justify universal cosmological claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid asserting universal negatives (impossibility) from experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The non-existence of a phenomenon within experience only shows no adequate cause has yet manifested; it does not prove absolute impossibility except in cases controlled by number/extension or by universal causality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve claims of impossibility for cases grounded in mathematical/extension laws or the universal law of causality. Do not infer that because something has never been observed it cannot exist — observation can only show absence of manifesting causes so far.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not resolve radically different phenomena into one element (illegitimate reduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fallacy of attempting to reduce qualitatively distinct phenomena (e.g., sensation, heat, light, consciousness) wholly to one type of phenomenon (e.g., motion, electricity) as if that removed their generic peculiarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It may be legitimate to show certain processes are conditions or causes of others, but demonstrating physical conditions does not thereby 'explain away' the distinctive nature of sensations or other qualitatively different phenomena. Even if motions precede sensation, the sensation remains a distinct kind of fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid simple enumeration (inductio per enumerationem simplicem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizing by mere enumeration of observed instances ('this A, that A, and other As are B; therefore every A is B') without elimination of alternatives is a childish and provisionary induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace enumeration by methods of separation and rejection (elimination) and seek negative instances sufficient to justify affirmative conclusions. Examples of the error: crude 'common-sense' maxims (e.g., 'whatsoever has never been, will never be') and societal stereotypes derived from limited observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish empirical laws from causal (ultimate) laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Confounding empirical generalizations (customary order of succession of events) with laws of cause and effect leads to overconfidence in empirical claims; empirical laws may be provisional and limited to space/time observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat empirical regularities as potentially local and contingent; investigate underlying causes before elevating empirical laws to ultimate status. Look for gradations/series in phenomena that can justify stronger empirical inferences; otherwise remain cautious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer causation from mere temporal or conjunctive association (post hoc / cum hoc ergo propter hoc)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferring that A causes B merely because A preceded or co-occurred with B is a vulgar empirical fallacy unless supported by elimination of alternatives or by known properties suggesting causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require additional evidence: elimination of other antecedents, or independent grounds to think the supposed cause has a tendency to produce the effect. Examples: attributing national prosperity to a single institution because prosperity was present under it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false theory (bad generalization a priori)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductively assigning one dominant cause or principle to explain complex phenomena while overlooking co-existing agents and conditions (e.g., seeking one universal principle of all disease), leading to systematic mis-explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of grand single-factor theories that ignore multiple interacting causes. Verify by seeking evidence that the supposed single agent actually has the known properties to produce the effects attributed to it; historical examples include mono-causal medical doctrines and analogous political/economic theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat analogical arguments as weak presumptions, not proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments from analogy infer that because cases are similar in some respects they may be similar in others; such inferences only provide a small, non-assignable increase in probability unless a connecting law is known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogy only to suggest hypotheses; do not overrate its probative force. Where possible, strengthen an analogy by showing that the shared property A is causally connected with the inferred property B (then the argument ceases to be mere analogy). Example: planets resembling Earth only slightly raise probability of inhabitants unless causal connection is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware false analogies and inferring similarity of one point from another
rubrics_metrics.description: A false analogy occurs when resemblance in one respect is taken to imply resemblance in another materially relevant respect, even when evidence may positively disconnect them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the point of resemblance is relevant to the inferred property; examine disanalogies that may undercut the analogy. Illustrated errors: inferring that despotic political government will work because paternal authority in a family 'works', or inferring sickness of a state from increased size of a metropolis; identify the missing relevant connecting circumstances (e.g., affection, wisdom) before inferring similarity.
